utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Djordjevic, could you please go to tab 151, and I would like us all to look at document D004-1705 on our screens. That's 911 on our 65 ter list. Just a moment, we're still waiting for the document to come up on our screens. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we should look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's page 1 of this document, at least that's what I had. So could you please go to next page. Yes, that's fine. Now, Mr. Djordjevic, here we can see a memo dated the 30th of April, 1999, from Assistant Minister Stojan Misic. So could you please tell us, briefly, what is this document about?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a notification sent to all border police stations and SUPs and the MUP staff in Pristina and also to some organisational units in the MUP headquarters by the assistant minister, Mr. Misic -- actually, a new war press card form -- format was established and the addressees of this dispatch were told that the new format was in force now. The previous one was no longer valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have this document exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D447.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, could we please look at D254.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That would be at tab 152, Mr. Djordjevic. Mr. Djordjevic, here we can see a memo from the 4th of May, 1999. You signed it. Could you please tell us what is this document about?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, orders were issued to all secretariats and all organisational units in the public security department and to the MUP staff in Pristina as to how to treat assignments related to the security of persons and places after the NATO air-strikes and the obligations that the members of the ministry had after those air-strikes. It is a reminder to all the secretariats and the organisational units as to how they should act if there are any attacks, how they should put out fires and provide help to any persons who were at risk because of the air-strikes and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, regarding your order yesterday - and that was about the admission of D443, a report at the -- in the office of the supreme commander of the 4th of May, 1999, published in "Politika" daily on the 5th of May, 1999 - I was actually wrong. On the 65 ter list provided by the Prosecution there is a piece of evidence, a memo written on the 6th of May, 1999, by the MUP staff and sent to all the secretariats in Kosovo and Metohija, to the PJP and the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit. Attached thereto was the text that we admitted into evidence yesterday. So now the Defence would be seeking to expand our 65 ter list to include this document. Now, I don't know whether this is an appropriate time to deal with that or perhaps we can do it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You wish to add the document now on the screen to your 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not the one that's on the screen. That one's already been admitted. But the 65 ter document of -- the Prosecution document, the number is 2159. It's on their 65 ter list. I don't know if we can maybe see it on the screen -- well, it's about to come up. Perhaps if we can scroll down so that we can see the body of the text in English. In Serbian we can see it, but we don't see it in Serbian. Could we please have page 2 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be added to the list, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I now tender it into evidence so that we get everything, so that -- under the same number, if this could be attached to D443. We want to have a single exhibit -- or perhaps if you prefer we can have two separate exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This will become part of Exhibit D443.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djordjevic, could you please go to tab 154.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D004-1586. That's 1779 on the Defence 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, we're about to see a dispatch dated the 12th of May, 1999, signed by Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic on our screens. So could you please wait for us to actually look at this dispatch once it's on our screens and then you can perhaps tell us what this dispatch is all about.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister sent this dispatch on the 12th of May to the border police stations and to the secretariats where border police stations were located, notifying them that they should improve the efficiency of the transportation of humanitarian relief, supplies, goods that are used for the production; in other words, to reduce the administrative procedures at the border to the minimum in order for the goods to reach their addressees as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please exhibit this document. I would like to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D448.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please look at document D008-2518.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That would be at tab 155.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it's 473 on the Defence 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djordjevic, we see a memo date the 7th of May, 1999, sent by the minister to the Supreme Command Staff. Could you please tell us what is this all about?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 7th of May, 1999, the minister sent to the Supreme Command Staff, to Colonel-General Ojdanic, who was the Chief of Staff, a memo telling him that in line with the previous agreement the -- he should actually let the minister of the interior have some assets, some weapons primarily that were needed by the police in light of constant NATO attacks on our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Djordjevic, could you please tell us, who was it in the ministry that actually made decisions, and who actually dealt with the procurement of materiel and equipment?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the general services administration. General Petar Zekovic was directly responsible to the minister. That was the administration that dealt with financial affairs and also with procurement of everything that was needed for the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And who could actually make the decision to procure some items?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all requests that pertained to equipment in the ministry were dealt with by the minister. He decided on all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D449.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D008-151 -- 2515. That's 472 on the Defence 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And that would be 156, your tab, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the request that we have seen, General Ojdanic issues an order dated the 12th of May to his administration for procurement. That administration was supposed to provide the equipment, the necessary equipment, to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would like to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D450.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like us to look at D008-2512. That's 471 on the Defence 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That would be at tab 157 for you, Mr. Djordjevic. Could you please tell us, briefly, what this document is all about?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now, this logistics sector that received an order from the Chief of the General Staff to provide the equipment issued an order to its subordinate unit, the unit that was actually supposed to provide the items, instructing it to do that by the 20th of May, 1999, and to report back about the compliance with the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D451, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we see D001-2933, 1206 is the 65 ter Defence list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: 158 tab in your binder. Mr. Djordjevic, we don't have a translation of this document, but please read from the first page so that we can see what this is about.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic, on the 12th of June, 1999, sent this letter to the Supreme Command Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, Colonel-General Dragoljub Ojdanic. He sent to him a survey of attacks of Albanian terrorists using mines and explosives in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija in the time-period from January 1, 1998, until the 6th of June, 1999, for their use. So this survey contains information about attacks during roughly one year.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D452, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, now we have come to the 12th of June. Yesterday you told us that on the eve of the Kumanovo Agreement you went to Pristina. Can you tell us, please, how and why did you go to Pristina, who else was there when you went there on the eve of Kumanovo Agreement?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at that point in time Kumanovo Agreement had already been signed, and there were responsibilities specified for the forces of Yugoslavia and Serbia, namely, for them to withdraw from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. Together with the minister on the 10th of June, we went to Kosovo, and a meeting was held at the staff with all the members of the staff and with chiefs of secretariats. At the meeting, we pointed out obligations that secretariats had in terms of withdrawal from Kosovo and what other tasks needed to be completed because that pull-out had to be completed within the following one or two days, or, rather, when NATO forces arrived at the border. Therefore, in accordance with the agreement that had been signed, the minister and General Stevanovic, who signed the agreement on behalf of the ministry delegation, spoke about those duties and obligations; and pursuant to those obligations, the secretariats acted in the following period and removed their personnel from Kosovo and Metohija into the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see P1209, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, it's tab 159 in your binder. We will now see a dispatch dated the 12th of June, 1999. Tell us, briefly, what is the content of this dispatch signed by you?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 12th of June, I sent a dispatch to all SUPs, to the staff, and to the heads of units within the ministry seat. I sent them this dispatch detailing which secretariat from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija would be relocated to the territory of which secretariat in the territory of Serbia. Based on this dispatch, the Nis SUP was to receive the entire equipment, weaponry, and everything else from the Pristina SUP; Kraljevo SUP was to receive all of the equipment and materiel of the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP; Kragujevac was to receive everything from the Pec SUP. So this is what this dispatch was about, which secretariats in Serbia would receive the equipment and everything else from the premises from Kosovo secretariats. And they were also to provide facilities for them to work. The other part of this dispatch deals with the members of "posebne" units who were coming back from Kosovo and Metohija. And there is also a provision here that all of them are to receive five days, that the review of troops and weapons was to be conducted, that people should be allowed to use their unused annual leave days, and that also certain compensation that was overdue needed to be paid to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see P1210.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, this is your letter dated the 27th of June, 1999. Could you please explain to us why this letter was drafted and what is this about.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the withdrawal of forces of the ministry from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, the assessment was that some activities of these forces from Kosovo would be aimed towards the secretariats -- would be linked with secretariats, and the territory that borders the territory of Kosovo, which was the territory of Vranje, Leskovac, Prokuplje, Novi Pazar, and Uzice Secretariats. Therefore, the secretariats from these areas were ordered to draft an evaluation. And all of this has to do with the fact that the Kumanovo Agreement provided for a land zone -- a land security zone in order to protect the territory of Serbia, as a result of which these secretariats were given certain obligations in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 008-0511. This is 909 off -- on the OTP 65 ter list -- or rather, on the Defence list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And this is tab 161 in your binder, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a criminal report or a criminal complaint filed on the 30th of April, 2001, against the minister, against me, and then under 3 there's a mistake. There should be Zoran Milic, not Stojan Milic, who is assistant chief of the police administration --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the second page in the English and in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You can continue.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So under 3 there's a mistake here. It should read Zoran Milic and not Stojan Milic, so a mistake in the name. A criminal report was filed against us. In relation to the minister it charged him with abuse of his position; for me -- it had something to do with the National Bank of Yugoslavia; the same charge related to me as well because I signed some receipts for athletes who participated in some competitions outside of Serbia, and they charged me with improper use of budget funds. This is the answers of the charges against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, please slowly, for the sake of the transcript, please tell us what this criminal report charged you with and what did -- what were the charges against the minister?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the minister, it says crime under Article 242, paragraphs 1 and 3, for abuse of power and for failure to discharge his duties, for failure to order the -- for failure to order that the National Bank of Yugoslavia receive certain funds in the amount of 490.000 marks; and as for me, they claimed that I abused my office by signing travel orders for athletes who represented an athletic club overseas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what happened afterwards, as far as you know, about -- in relation to this criminal report which was submitted to the district prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that the entire financial documentation of this athletic club, whose chairman I was, was inspected by the inspectors of the crime investigations police and various other services; and following investigation, they established that I signed these receipts and travel orders, and this is what they put in this criminal report. At that point in time I did not see this criminal report. I learned of this investigation and that they were preparing to arrest me only afterwards. This is what the situation is regarding this criminal report and charges against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Under Article 41 of the ministry of -- or rather, of the Law on Internal Affairs, you went into early retirement. Did you; and, if so, when did you sign the request to retire?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was retired on the 3rd of May. In the course of the day --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's an appalling -- an appalling leading question, having regard to what the evidence has been so far. I would ask through the Court that counsel not continue to lead anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, if you could observe that please, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's -- I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead and explain to us how it is that you came to retire.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already mentioned this, but I will repeat it now. I held the position in the co-ordination centre in the south of Serbia, which dealt with the situation in the land security zone that I've mentioned earlier. I was retired on the 3rd of May without my knowledge; I didn't know that they retired me. In the evening, after the meetings in the co-ordination centre were over, General Lukic called me to tell me that I had been retired earlier during that day and that I should report to him on the following day to receive the paperwork -- the decision on my retirement. I went to see him. And up until that time -- up until he called me, I had no idea that I had been retired. When I arrived in the office, there was a request, my request, addressed to the minister for retirement -- for early retirement, in accordance with the provisions of the law. That was -- that request was already written, and I simply signed it, given that the decision on my retirement had already been issued. I didn't want to cause any problems. If the state had decided to retire me, I was willing to accept it. I signed all the paperwork, received all the compensation that was due to me, and this is how my work with the ministry ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for enabling me to examine my client in this extent and for this period of time. And prior to that, I would like to ask that the last document on the screen be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document D008-0511 will be Exhibit D453.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you then, Mr. Djurdjic. When it's convenient, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours, and good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You told us that you got an LLB degree at some point in time. At what year was that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I graduated in 1971 at the Faculty of Law in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did that degree make you lawyer? By that I mean were you then entitled to practice law in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following the completion of the law degree, I was given a title of a lawyer; but immediately after that, within a month, I started working for the Ministry of the Interior, where I worked until my retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I saw from one of the documents that you were shown earlier, D393, that at some point in time you were chief of inspectorate for internal control of lawfulness of work. Do you remember when you were appointed to that position?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that was in 1990 and that I remained in that position of the chief of the inspectorate for internal control within the Ministry of the Interior for about a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, what did your task or what did your job in that position entail?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person in that position had a duty to establish the lawfulness of actions of members of the ministry and also some units of the ministry, some organisational units of the ministry. For example, if there was a group within the ministry that acted beyond what the law permits, then it was my duty to look into that and to inform the senior management of the ministry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In other words, your responsibilities at that time involved investigating allegations that members of the ministry had committed crimes?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Investigations were conducted by relevant investigative bodies pursuant to criminal reports that had been filed, and independently from any criminal proceedings there were a lot of complaints by citizens that did not relate to crimes committed by members of the ministry but some other inappropriate acts on their behalf. So I had to look into that, to respond to the complaining party, and to draft reports for the ministry. The entire domain of criminal conduct was in -- was within the jurisdiction of relevant state bodies --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- any secretariat within the ministry could file criminal reports if they learned --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks. I think you have answered the question. You weren't responsible for investigating allegations of crime. Now, later on, I see from the history, from your personal history, you eventually became the acting chief of the RJB, the public security department. Can you remind us what year that was?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received the decision, I think, on the 1st of June, 1977 [as interpreted], and sometime in January of 1978 [as interpreted] I received a decision for the chief of the public security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I take it that would be 1997 and 1998, not as I see the transcript here saying 1977 and 1978.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1997. And then in 1998 I received this other decree appointing me as the chief of the RJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we have a look at one of the documents relating to that, that is D421.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Here I see you're promoted to the rank of colonel-general of police from lieutenant-general. Is there a rank --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it appears to me that we are not looking at the same document in B/C/S and in the English version. We can see that the date in the English version is the 28th of March, 1997, whereas the Serbian version is from July 1997. Now, perhaps -- now it's been changed. Maybe now it's the correct version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, look on the Serbian version. If we could scroll down and look at the date because there might be a mistake in the English copy. So just tell us the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm reminded that when this was tendered the discrepancy of dates was pointed out and there was going to be a correct translation obtained and substituted. It is the date of the heading of the document that is wrong, not the date at the end of it in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could we just go to the end of the document and get the correct date. That's page 2 in English document -- or page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 6th of July, 1997, you were promoted to colonel-general, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was there any higher rank that a member of the MUP could attain?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In keeping with the regulations in force at the time, that was the highest rank in the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could go back to page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We see that General Stevanovic and General Markovic were promoted to major-general. Were they always thereafter subordinate to you in rank in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all as you've indicated, I don't think that this is what should be in the English version. First of all, it’s Obrad Stevanovic, not Stepanovic, as it says here. And secondly, they were promoted to the rank of lieutenant-general. Their previous rank had been major-general. So they were already major-generals, and they were promoted to the rank of lieutenant-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And the question is that after that they remained at a lower rank than the one you had while you remained in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, each held the rank for which he was commissioned, and yes, their ranks were below mine. But...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -– as each advanced, he received...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that doesn't mean that I was their superior officer because I had a higher rank. It's a completely different subject. The fact that I was lieutenant -- that I was a colonel-general didn't mean that I was the superior officer to a lieutenant-general, unlike in the army. But even in the army, the rank does not guarantee that somebody is, in fact, a superior officer to another person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at page 17, line 3, in the transcript, we have -- what is stated in the transcript was that their ranks were subordinate to his, where, in fact, he said that their ranks were lower than his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is clear from the document that the two named people, Stevanovic and Markovic, were promoted to the rank of lieutenant-general at the same time that the accused, who had been a lieutenant-general, was promoted to the rank of colonel-general. We are having a lot of discussion consequent on that getting us nowhere. I think if we moved on, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, who recommended you for promotion to colonel-general?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's Mr. Stojiljkovic at the time?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And who appointed you to head of the RJB?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In line with his powers under the law, that was Minister Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now if I could move on to the circumstances of your retirement. You told us that you were pensioned off even before you had met the prerequisites for retirement. In May 2001 you are saying you had not met the prerequisites for retirement?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Ministry of the Interior where you had accelerated pension plans, you had to serve for 30 years to get a full pension. That's 40 years of normal pensionable career and then you were entitled to a full pension. At the time when I retired, I did not meet this prerequisite. You could, however, get early retirement if you met some other prerequisites, which I did. So for all intents and purposes, I would have had to have worked one and a half year to get a full pension; however, I retired in line with the current regulations. I was entitled to a pension and the -- my superiors in the ministry took an opportunity to retire me, and I was fine with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at 05221. It's the Prosecution's 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You signed this request?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you write it?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't write this. On the 30th of April I was in Bujanovac, which is 350 kilometres away from Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, I just asked you if you wrote this or not. The answer is: No, you did not. Who wrote it, do you know?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. When I came to see General Lukic, who was the chief of the department, to receive the decision on my retirement, he gave me this request for signature, for my signature, because this was a prerequisite for me getting the pension. For the minister to issue his decision, we had to have my request for retirement in the file, in my file.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, you're going way beyond the questions that I'm asking you. Just focus on what I ask you and answer them directly, please. When you signed this, you were aware that you would not be entitled to a full pension, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm objecting to an erroneous question. First of all, the question is -- was: Were you aware that you were not entitled to a full pension. We have to deal with the legal categories that exist here. We have early retirement under Article 41; we have the old age --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, you are in the process of trying to give a legal explanation, which might answer the question put by counsel to the witness. We're going to get along a lot better and a lot faster if you leave it to the witness to answer. If you find there is something incomplete or unsatisfactory in the answer, you may deal with it in re-examination. We cannot get into the habit of you standing and adding some view of your own after the witness has dealt with the question. If we could observe that, it will enable us to move more quickly. Carry on, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you -- or did General Lukic tell you who prepared the letter, that is, your letter requested retirement?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Prior to signing this letter, did you discuss your retirement or your dismissal, as you put it, on more than one occasion with the minister?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never discussed this topic with the minister, and, in fact, I didn't see him either before or after I received the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did Sreten Lukic tell you why you were going to be pensioned off or dismissed by the minister at a lower pension than you would have been entitled to?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that one day before, the retirement procedure had already been completed. I had no idea about it. Sreten Lukic simply handed me the decision without providing any reasons, any explanations. I received the decision --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Simple question, simple answer. Did Sreten Lukic tell you why you were being retired? So you can tell me he did or he did not. I didn't ask for an explanation.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did anybody tell you why you were going to be retired after 30 years in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you inquire of anybody who may have participated in that decision with the minister as to why you would be retired after 30 years in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't inquire because the decision had already been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, the decision was made, but you said it was necessary for you to sign the request in order to get your pension. If you did not sign the request, you would have been entitled to appeal the decision, would you not?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, the minister represents the state --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Djordjevic --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm listening --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let's take it step by step. Would you not have been entitled to appeal the decision to dismiss you after 30 years, had you not signed the request?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really tell you. I think I may have been entitled, but I can't really be sure. I can't quote the relevant articles. And I'm not sure whether I had the right to appeal in such a case or not. I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, we have seen and we will see later on many orders you signed transferring people, transferring SUP chiefs from one position to another, in which the orders clearly state that they had a certain amount of days in order to appeal that decision. I ask you again: Weren't you, a lawyer, after 30 years of service, aware that you would have been entitled to appeal your decision -- or, I'm sorry, appeal the decision to dismiss you?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any rate, I think that I was entitled to appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Of course. Just about that time in May 2001, the media in Serbia and in the world had started to publish reports on the discovery of hundreds of corpses at Batajnica near Belgrade. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that it was the case. Now, whether Batajnica was mentioned or not, I can't really tell you. But I know that there were reports for the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you know -- you were involved in the disposal of those bodies in some way, did you not?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't involved in the operation to remove the bodies. I explained to you my role, and I will also have an opportunity to answer your questions in this regard. My task was -- well, we'll discuss this later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. When you were retired or dismissed, as you put it, and you accepted that, you knew not only that --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- I'm trying to rephrase the question in a more simple way. At the time you retired, 1st of May, 2001, not only was the fact that bodies had been found at the Danube being circulated in the press in Serbia, but you knew that you had a role in the whole thing, in the whole affair, to conceal the bodies; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did play a certain role, but I've explained what kind of a role it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Back to your background. In 1998 when you were in Kosovo, did you have a radio call-sign?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: During your evidence I think you told us that while you were down there in Kosovo during those operations, everybody had call-signs, all the senior persons had radio call-signs; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you what my call-sign was: It was Morava 2 or Morava 3. That was the call-sign for my post. That was used regularly, in regular work in Belgrade. I never used it in Kosovo, however, and the officers in command of the units had their own call-signs. The staff had its call-signs, and those who were directly involved in the performance of certain tasks had their own call-signs. But in 1998, not only did I not have a call-sign that was adapted to those circumstances, I didn't have a radio station at all at my disposal. I did not have a radio when I went down there --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and I couldn't have had a call-sign. I didn't have any need for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In 1999 your call-sign was -- is it Morava? Could you tell us what the call-sign was again, please?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was Morava 2 or Morava 3. I really can't remember. The minister was Morava 1, the RJB chief is the next call-sign in line, and the RDB chief the next. There were documents specifying the call-signs for all MUP personnel in regular circumstances, in day-to-day business.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So in 1999 your call-sign would be Morava 2?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The moment I was appointed the chief of the RJB -- well, the call-sign for the RJB chief was always Morava 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So why couldn't you use that in Kosovo if you were down there in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no need for me to use the call-sign. I had other ways to communicate. But when I was in Kosovo, I never used the call-sign, never ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That last document that I showed to the witness, his request for retirement, could that be received -- it has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, Your Honours, I'm just advised that it was already admitted as part of the decision on the bar table motion yesterday or this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So that is, for the record, P1470. Could we look at 65 ter 06011.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We see here, Mr. Djordjevic, the cover page of the "Official Gazette" for the 9th of June, 1999. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now I'd like to go to page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that two translations were put in e-court. One, which we are seeing now, is part of the cover page. Could we look at the second translation in e-court which takes us to a later part of that, of the gazette for that day which is a long document. And this is a decree on decoration, and it is at page 11 of the gazette. I don't know if we could find that in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that what you have before you, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have these rules, but they do not deal with these issues at all. I think that this is June and not July -- oh, yes, I see now the presidential decree of the president of the FRY. That's probably what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could it be enlarged, please, so that I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps you can scroll up a little bit more. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a decree of the President of the FRY, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Mr. Milosevic, of the 9th of July, 1999, pursuant to the constitution and other laws of the federal republic awarding decorations for the courage, determination, and discipline exhibited in discharging security tasks of combatting terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija and in defending the country from aggression, serving as examples to other members -- to other units and police members. The award of national hero was awarded to the 124th Intervention Brigade. Do you recall that, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where was this brigade operational during the war?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 124th Intervention Brigade of the PJPs comprised members of the police force, of the secretariats of the interior from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. And in 1998 and in 1999, this brigade carried out tasks in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I just want you to focus on what I'm asking you. I'm asking you about the period of the war, because that is what the decorations were about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we turn to the next page in English --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to highlight the issue of the defence of the country from the aggression. That was the reason why these decorations and awards were given by the then-president. So this isn't only about commanding police units and demonstrating courage in carrying out the tasks aimed at suppressing terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija but also for the defence of the country against the aggression. And the country at the time was the FRY which was attacked, and it was attacked throughout its territory. I was responsible for one part of the territory, and it's probably the reason why my name came up for this decoration and why I was ultimately awarded this decoration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You know, Mr. Djordjevic, I did not ask you that. You pre-empted me. You look at the persons awarded the Order of the Yugoslav Flag, First Class, you see your name, the first name, and you also see Lieutenants-General Obrad Stevanovic and Sreten Lukic. Where were Obrad Stevanovic and Sreten Lukic operational during the war, March to June 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sreten Lukic was head of the MUP staff for suppression of terrorism, and he was located in Pristina. Obrad Stevanovic, pursuant to the decision of the minister, also went to Kosovo on the first day of the war based on the minister's orders and stayed there throughout most of the time until the signing of the Kumanovo Agreement and until the pull-out of forces was completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Look at the persons who received the Order of the Yugoslav Flag, Second Class. Where were they assigned to during the war? It starts with Zivaljevic.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them were commanders of some units of PJPs, all of these people listed here. And depending on their rotation periods, they would spend a certain period of time with their units in Kosovo. I can explain each case individually. Colonel Zivaljevic from the Belgrade SUP was there in the role of --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Go on, go on.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of a contingent of the Belgrade PJP. Grekulovic, Srdjan, was also a commander of a detachment. The same goes for Radoslav Mitrovic. And Radislav Stalevic was commander of the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit in Pristina. Branko Prljevic was also a commander of a unit in PJP from the territory of Uzice. Zarko Brakovic, who was a witness here, was the commander of a brigade. And Buha was a commander of the other contingent of the Belgrade PJP. And Milorad Lukovic was a commander of the RDB unit for special operations, JSO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And all of them were active in Kosovo during the war, exhibiting and discharging security duties for combatting terrorism, as the president of the republic put it. Right?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Look at the persons who received the Order of the Yugoslav Flag, Third Class.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all of them were senior officers within those units of PJPs. I can see Zivko Trajkovic there, who was a commander of a Special Anti-Terrorist Unit of the MUP of Serbia; and Zoran Simovic, who was the commander of the Belgrade contingent of the SAJ. The rest of them are from PJPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Also exhibiting courage and determination in discharging security tasks combatting terrorism in Kosovo, all of them; right?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And we could go on and on and on. But we have looked at the -- those who received the highest prizes. You were explaining to me earlier that the award was also for defending the country. Were there not other assistant ministers, like Zekovic - is it Zekovic? - Misic --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- who were also engaged in tasks, defending the country, in places outside of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This same Order of the Yugoslav Flag, Third Class, is the decoration that Markovic received and another person. Most likely, at that point in time, the minister proposed them because the role of other assistant ministers wasn't that significant. They were in charge, and they reported to the minister for the matters that had nothing to do with direct defence of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you're saying their roles were insignificant, they did not deserve commendations as you did?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that they dealt with insignificant matters, no. They worked on matters that were significant for the ministry, but they were not related to the defence of the country. And in my view, those were the reasons for the minister to draft the proposal with these names. It is possible that they received another kind of a decoration that was appropriate for the roles that they had at that time. I can't remember whether they were decorated as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I think I mentioned Zekovic and Misic. I had a note here for another assistant minister apart from Mr. Markovic, but I can't find it. Who was the other assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time, Nikola Curcic was assistant minister, who was also director of the institute and deputy chief of the state security department. So he was Rade Markovic's deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. So the minister -- and this is your evidence - the minister, Mr. Stojiljkovic, in making the recommendation to the president of the country for persons to receive some of the highest awards the country can give, recommended all these persons who were engaged in combatting terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija for that role, and you were the only person in this list who had no participation in combatting terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija during the war in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister wasn't in charge of combatting terrorism, neither was Rade Markovic, and they were decorated, both of them. But in order for these persons to be proposed for a decoration -- the only person entitled to put their names up was the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what I'm -- all I've asked you is that of all of the persons we have seen receive the highest awards, Order of National Hero, Order of the Yugoslav Flag, First Class, Second Class, and Third Class, and the Order of Merit for the FRY, Second Class, all of them but you were in Kosovo in 1999; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have explained my role already. Let me just say this: If we were to look at this list in its entirety, you will see that there are also members of various secretariats outside of Kosovo on it too but they received some lower decorations. When proposing people for these awards, the main criteria that the minister used was whether these people were involved in combatting terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija; and as a rule they received more decorations. However, in this list there are also other people from other areas within Serbia, other SUPs, and they received some other decorations that were not of such a high level.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is what I'm talking about, the people who got the highest awards. I suggest to you, Mr. Djordjevic, that the prime minister -- sorry, the President, Milosevic, made these awards to persons who were directly involved in the fight in Kosovo and Metohija, including you, and that you deserved the award because you had overall responsibility for the units in Kosovo and Metohija. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is your construct; that does not correspond to the truth. I was responsible for the situation in Serbia outside of Kosovo and Metohija, and other people were responsible for the situation in Kosovo and Metohija and engagement of all units in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Convenient time, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If that's convenient, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Isn't it time? I was wondering if it was the time. Yes, it is convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are over time. I've been waiting for a suitable break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the first break now and resume at 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, did you recommend for decorations any of the persons who received any of the higher awards that we referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not personally --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because there's a system stipulated by the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we -- but I tender this document and ask that it be received in evidence and given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P1506.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Djordjevic, that Mr. -- or former VJ general, Vasiljevic, came here and testified about a variety of things, including meetings that he had with the president of the republic, President Milosevic; and he said that President Milosevic spoke of you and also of the Minister Stojiljkovic as clearly the persons most responsible or who bear -- to use his words, he said President Milosevic referred to you and to the minister Stojiljkovic as the persons who bear the highest responsibility for the use of the MUP forces in Kosovo. And this was in the middle of May 1999 that Mr. Vasiljevic was referring to. Do you know of any information that would be available --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, rather than jumping to my feet and constantly objecting, let me do it now. If something is being quoted, could we please have a reference in the transcript to the verbatim words of Mr. Vasiljevic, because several times already the formulations of Mr. Stamp do not correspond to what I remember the evidence to be when he's quoting words of some other witnesses. So could we please have the reference and see the exact words of Mr. Vasiljevic, and could that be put to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think if you could observe that, Mr. Stamp, it would be helpful. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours. This is at 5688 of the transcript of the 8th of June, lines 5 to 15, which can be checked, but I won't read them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General Vasiljevic said that Mr. Milosevic in mid-May 1999 referred to you; Obrad, that's Mr. Obrad Stevanovic; and the Minister Stojiljkovic as, at line 13: "... the persons who bear the highest responsibility for the use of the MUP forces in Kosovo." Do you know what information was available to the president of the republic that would cause him to arrive at a conclusion that you, along with the minister and Assistant Minister Stevanovic, bore the highest responsibility for the use of the MUP forces?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the outset, let me say that several days prior to that meeting - which, by the way, I did not attend nor do I know what transpired there - that after several years in retirement, Vasiljevic started working again, and then after three or four days of being back to work, he became an expert for all matters, including the internal affairs --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so I did not attend this meeting. I don't know the context in which this discussion was held --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, I'm just asking you to comment on the evidence. What you have said here about Mr. Vasiljevic, he has already testified about how he became involved in this. Just focus on the question. Do you know what information was available to the president of the republic that could cause him to conclude that you, Mr. Stojiljkovic, and Mr. Stevanovic were the persons who bore the highest responsibility for the use of MUP forces in Kosovo during the war in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot give comments on the comments and conclusions of Vasiljevic. He said that I attended the meeting on the 1st of June, but I didn't. Now, as to what notes he made at that meeting with President Milosevic, I don't know. I was not present at the meeting; I don't know what the topic of the discussion was. And it's quite natural that presidents of Yugoslavia and Serbia knew who held what positions, who was chief of which department, and that they knew what their role in general terms was within the state administration system.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could have a look at P357. That is the rules of internal organisation for the MUP. And if we could find Article 54 in both the English and the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It says that the: "Departments shall be controlled by the chiefs of departments." Can I take it that according to the rules of internal organisation of the MUP, the public service department was under these rules controlled by you, the chief of the department?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the rules - I'm just speaking about the rules now - they don't make any distinction between public service department units inside or outside of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand your question. These rules specify the organisation of the RJB and they supply to the entire territory of Serbia. We already spoke about that. There were territorial units and those were secretariats, and there was secretariats everywhere, both in Serbia and in Kosovo and everywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. So I ask you now, following from that, are you saying that you as the highest-ranking professional police officer in Serbia, a lawyer, and the chief of the RJB, had no responsibility for MUP units that were operational in Kosovo in 1999? Are you disowning these units?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You say that ultimately these units in 1999 were not under your direction as chief of the RJB? Do you say that, sir, as a general, as a colonel-general, that the men in Kosovo who were fighting in 1999, you disown them? You wash your hands of them?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not washing my hands of anything or anyone. These people who were fighting in Kosovo, they continued to be personnel of the RJB; but pursuant to a decision of the minister, they were seconded to other structures that planned and exercised command over them in the performance of various combat tasks. So these units that were involved in anti-terrorist and combat actions in 1999, I did not have any power over them. I did not issue a single task to them, a task that would have to do with their activities. Those tasks were entrusted to other people by the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We'll get to the command, the direct command, in Kosovo later on. I just want to be absolutely clear, General, that you are saying that notwithstanding your position under the law, under the rules, and your rank as a general -- a colonel-general, and notwithstanding that it might be that they were commanded in individual operations by persons in Kosovo, you are saying that you have no responsibility for the police who were engaged in the defence of the country and the anti-terrorist operations in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not something that I think. That's how it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for sure we will reach some documents that will show that quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you disown them or disclaim any responsibility for them because you know that they were engaged in massive crimes against humanity in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please ask me one question at a time in order for me to be able to give you precise answers. You're using heavy words, and I can't really grasp their full meaning at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you disown or disclaim responsibility for the MUP personnel in Kosovo in 1999 because you are aware that they were engaged in massive war crimes and crimes against humanity at that time? Is that why you tell us, General, that you have no responsibility for them?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me say that I don't know -- I don't have any information as to who committed what kind of crime, small- or large-scale. I know about the crime in Podujevo. That's the only crime that I'm aware of. So I don't know who committed crimes. I don't have any information to that effect. I'm not disowning those -- the personnel of the RJB that were part of the SAJ or the PJPs at the time who performed some tasks in Kosovo. I'm not disowning them because they may have committed some crimes. I'm only saying that pursuant to a decision of the minister their entire operation, their entire activities in that area were under the responsibility of other people who were in turn directly responsible to the minister. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You discussed earlier in your testimony your presence in Kosovo in 1998, and I think you said that your role down there was as an observer, to represent the minister as an observer. I'd like to show you what General Lukic, who was the head of the staff down there, said about your role down there and ask you to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at 0948 or 00948.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell me the reference where General Lukic said that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. It's coming up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think there's a corrected version in e-court. Perhaps you could try to find that. Yes, that's it. Could we look at page 41. That is not the correct version, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while it is coming up, Mr. Djordjevic, was Mr. Stevanovic the commander of the special unit in Kosovo in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, he was not. He was the commander of the PJPs at an earlier time, but at that time he was in Kosovo in his capacity as the assistant minister. When I was in Kosovo, I was not merely an observer. On the order of the minister, it was my task to get involved and to provide assistance in the activities being carried out down there and to give my contribution to the success of the anti-terrorist activity. So I was not merely an observer down there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, first could I observe that there appear to be two quite different documents on the screen. Could you attend to which it is that you're intending the witness to see. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have now come to the area where the interviews provided by suspects are about to be used. Those interviews have already been tender into evidence; but following objections by the Defence, the Chamber did not admit them into evidence. I know that under your decision issued in the course of the Prosecution case questions can be asked about some certain circumstances, but I think that it is inappropriate for this document to be shown to the witness and to be actually admitted into evidence in this way. It's not just one interview. This is the -- these are interviews provided by three more suspects, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Lukic, Mr. Pavkovic, and Mr. Lazarevic, and an interview with Mr. Milutinovic. And it was your position in your decision IT-05-87/7 of the 28th of April, 2009, and you provided your statement of reasons. I don't think that this is proper foundation for the use of this document. Yes, the Prosecution can ask questions about some circumstances, but these documents cannot be used in this way. I, in particular, object to the admission of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. At the moment there is no suggestion they be admitted. You, Mr. Stamp, might tell us what it is you are intending to refer to and what use you intend to try to make of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I indicated earlier, I wish to show him what Mr. Lukic said and ask him to comment on it, whether or not that reflects his memory of what the situation was at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this something you say was said by Mr. Lukic when interviewed?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And was he then interviewed as a suspect?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. This is Mr. Lukic's responses to questions in a suspect interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And has he since given evidence about this subject matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic? No, no, he has not. So at this stage the situation is merely to inquire of the witness whether or not what Mr. Lukic said reflects his recollection of the circumstances that prevailed at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Am I correct in understanding that Mr. Lukic is not foreshadowed as a Defence witness and you have not called him?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No -- well, we have not called him, and he's not on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, having considered Mr. Djurdjic's objection, the Chamber is of the view that you may properly make some use of this document for the purposes of cross-examination, but that the use you may properly make is a limited one, that is, for example, inviting the witness to read a particular portion and asking for the witness's comment on that portion, being for the witness then to comment if and as he chooses. And the document itself does not become evidence nor should you take the course of reading into the transcript that part of the document which you want the witness to read. Is that in accordance with your understandings and expectations?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I would -- I'm obliged to be able to use it, and I'll abide by that. I just want to know -- perhaps I could get some assistance as to how -- I just want to be sure that he reads the parts that I am -- I want to refer to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's difficult without --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- you should understand my comment to allow you, for example, to say, "Look in the middle of the page, the section commencing in English 'all police units ... ' and ending with 'Chief of Staff,'" would you read that and should you wish to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours, I'll proceed in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, you see in the middle of the page a section that commences with: "All police units ..." and ends with "the staff." Do you see what Mr. Lukic was saying there?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "All the forces" -- or rather, "forces, all the police units, including the original, parent, secretariats, had as their primary task curbing terrorism. The task of the staff was, therefore, to co-ordinate" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, you're reading the thing -- you don't need to read it aloud. I'm just asking you to look at it, read it, and if you could comment on it, firstly, by telling us whether you agree with it and tell us what you agree with.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what I see here, I see an interpretation of Mr. Lukic of those forces and the role of the staff, and we have seen very specific orders and tasks given to the staff by the minister and the obligations that stemmed from it. So I think what he's saying here does not really reflect the situation on the ground and the obligations that the staff had vis-à-vis the seconded units, the attached units, and all the other items that are contained in the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In other words, you don't agree with Mr. Lukic that there was a dual responsibility of the special units, both to the commander of the units and also to the head of staff?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now you're talking about the unit commanders. I don't know what commander you have in mind, but, at any rate, there was no dual responsibility as we can see in what Mr. Lukic is saying, and this is just his interpretation. The order issued by the minister specified in no uncertain terms who exercises control, who exercises command, who plans the tasks. So really ... I think that this does not correspond to the actual situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. If you could look at that other section just below that where Mr. Lukic is asked who had primacy. Just read that and read his answer below that where he refers to you and to Mr. Stevanovic and tell us if that accords with your memory as to the circumstances there in Kosovo as to who had primacy in leading the MUP forces.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is not saying about who has primacy. He merely says that Obrad Stevanovic and myself were there, but he's not saying who had primacy there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I think I have to ask you this: You see he's asked who had primacy, and in response to that question he says that both yourself and Mr. Stevanovic were there with him.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I said. He said that we were there with him, but he didn't say who had primacy. He didn't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next page and see him elaborating a little bit further. You see him continuing with his answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Mr. Stamp. Your Honour, can we be given the page numbers that are shown to the witness so that we could use it in re-direct because I don't see the page number here. I know what the document is, but I can't find the page itself. So could we please have the page reference because I -- you know how many pages we will have here and then it will be difficult for me to follow in my re-district.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, the page reference is right on the top of the screen, it's page 42 of the exhibit. And this is an exhibit that was specially corrected --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp -- [B/C/S on English channel] ... be able to read the page number, it would help Mr. Djurdjic, it would help the Chamber, and it would help the record if you indicate what you have not done so far, that the record that you have was that of an interview, where it was given, on such and such a date, the Office of the Prosecutor against General Sreten Lukic, and that you are referring to page so and so of that record. And we would, in due course, have it marked for identification so that it will be possible, both in re-examination and during final address and, if it should become the case, during any appeal for people to identify what it was that the witness was commenting on. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I thought -- well -- very well. I'll proceed in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is page 42 of this suspect interview with Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Given when and where?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 21st of May, 2002, at his office in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see here Mr. Lukic continues in an explanation by saying - and that is in answer to the question who had primacy down there - he spoke about this. Do you have any comment on his answer there?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I have a comment. First of all, he's talking here about hierarchy. In this specific case, we can discuss hierarchy for at least an hour. This hierarchy, as he perceives it, had nothing to do with the situation on the ground. So he is making a total mix-up of everything. So it was not clear what he wanted here to say. I completely don't understand what he wanted to say. These are his statements that I, at this point, really cannot make a head or tail of because they are totally beyond the actual situation on the ground, both with respect to his responsibility and the responsibility of General Stevanovic and myself in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, having regard to the last objection, before I would ask this question I would just indicate to the Court what I propose to do. And this is something which, I recall, has been done by the Defence in their cross-examination. I'm going to read to the witness a sentence from the testimony of Dusko Adamovic in a previous trial and ask him to comment on that. Dusko Adamovic was a member of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've mentioned a previous trial. Which trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That was the trial of Milutinovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that this is not on the Prosecution's list that was provided to us as the list to be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Were it on the list, would you object?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, had it been on the list, it wouldn't have any objection to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it's something you did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I know that. But I think that I asked my questions on the basis of these statements and the witnesses responded, but I didn't do it in that way. However, as it is, it's up to you to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It often is, Mr. Djurdjic. Mr. Stamp --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He has objected that it is not on your list.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, it is not on the list. I propose to do it because I saw that referring to the previous testimony of witnesses - I've seen it in the past - was something that was done in cross-examination. I just wish to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you suggest that you understood it was not necessary to identify previous testimony on your list for the purposes of giving notice?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. I -- and what I merely wish to do is to read to him one sentence from the testimony of somebody and ask him if he agrees with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
