utterances.text: I appreciate that, but we're moving on to the -- a related -- another issue, that is, whether you are required to give notice of this course and whether you have done so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going off practice. I have seen before, in the course of this trial, where statements or documents that persons have given was used in cross-examination and -- but it wasn't tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Were they the subject of notice of use?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you're saying you are in all respects doing as Mr. Djurdjic or Mr. Djordjevic did in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. And I -- and not only both of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Anything further, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, this notice was required by us to enable us to discuss it with the accused when we had time for that in preparation for re-direct. The Defence has used information from certain documents and statements, but without using the statement itself. We just quoted certain circumstances and asked the witness to comment on the circumstances without citing the provenance. For example, do you know whether there was any meeting between Mr. Walker and the Russian defence minister? And the witness says either yes or no. Now what we have here is something that we object to due to the fact that neither the Defence nor the accused received any notice in advance thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, subject to the sorts of limitations that we have been commenting on earlier and if necessary we will develop them further, you may proceed as you propose.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know what role Dusko Adamovic occupied during the summer offensive in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a member of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you comment on this? He said that before the map excerpts were distributed to the PJP commanders and before anti-terrorist operations were carried out, there was -- there were meetings with the commanders of the detachments and the chiefs of the SUPs, with -- the assistant ministers, Generals Djordjevic and General Obrad Stevanovic, told the officers about the tasks that they were to follow. Is that a correct representation of what occurred at that time in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 22nd of July, this meeting was held, the one that I suppose Dusko Adamovic speaks about and the one that he attended. At this meeting, we discussed and conveyed the obligations that we had received on the previous day from the minister, and they referred to how to comply with the plan of anti-terrorist activities in Kosovo. And in that respect, in the broadest sense of the word, the chiefs of SUPs were informed as well as the detachment commanders of PJPs and the special unit. And also present there was - if I'm not mistaken - the special ops commander from the state security department. In this meeting, we informed all present about their forthcoming tasks and obligations with relation to the plan. So this meeting did take place, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And were there further meetings, later meetings, because Mr. Adamovic speaks of meetings, where either yourself or General Stevanovic told the officers about the tasks that they were to follow during operations?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were some meetings. Some of them I attended, but most of them were attended by Obrad. The obligations that the staff had were explained by the head of the staff. We as assistant ministers, if we had any remarks or objections or any additions to make, were contributing to the debate in that way. Sometimes minister was present there, and he conveyed to General Stevanovic to pass on his orders to the fore. Dusko Adamovic was in all of these meetings. Therefore, our participation, the two assistants, was not so prominent in that respect when it came to fundamental obligations of the staff. These fundamental obligations vis-à-vis the units deployed there were on the part of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you said that you were sometimes out in the field when operations, more important operations were being conducted, you were out in the field of commanders. Is that -- is my memory of what you said correct?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's always something in between. I spoke about lots of things that were not mentioned there. I said that my commitment was pursuant to minister's orders in the field, not only with the commanders but also with the secretariats and the organisational units of the secretariats. So according to the minister's orders, I was more focused on how things were evolving on the field, to provide assistance if necessary, and to provide a secure -- a better cohesion in the performance of these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One operation or one instance in particular that you've testified about was one which occurred towards the end of September in Decani near Istinic. And you said a large-scale operation was being carried out in the area of Jablanica and Glodjane. The action was part of the final operations. When you say "large-scale," how many troops were involved or how many MUP members were involved in that operation?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at this moment, I really cannot say. I think there must be documents that provided for the total number of troops to be used, but I cannot say anything precisely. Maybe two or three PJP detachments took place, et cetera, but I really cannot tell you anything more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About how many members were in a detachment?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know these exact numbers. It may have been 500, but it depended on -- depended on the actual situation. Maybe the one in Kosovo was stronger. I really didn't follow these matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I don't know their exact numbers really.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's fine. I asked you approximately how many, and that's fine. You said that present with you was somebody by the name of Mrksic. Who was he? What was his position?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Mircic. He was the chief of the OUP Decani, that's the internal affairs organ, and Decani's the area where this operation took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said that he proposed to you that somebody should go into the villages and talk to the people to see if there -- the situation could be solved in a peaceful way. And you -- you nod that that's correct?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you accepted the proposal?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And stopped the operation and the matter was resolved and many lives were saved?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't exactly how it happened. This man proposed to go there and talk to the people there. He did that. The barricades were abandoned, there was no resistance to the police, and practically with the cease of the resistance and without any fighting with the police the operation ended. It wasn't I who stopped the operation. Since there was no resistance, no shooting at the police, this operation ended because each and every operation actually had the aim to target the terrorists and to crush their resistance. With the active participation of the chief of the OUP, this armed clash was avoided, and, thereby, the operation ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I -- tell me if my understanding is correct. I understood you to say that the operation was stopped and you waited until 1600 hours to see if the proposals would be accepted. That is not correct? You didn't say that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operation covered a wider area. Therefore, by the time the information arrived that they would fulfil the promise that they would leave the barricades and not put any resistance to the police, it was close to 1600 hours when the entire operation was finished; however, the units were still there. They were not close to the Istinic village where there were many civilians. Later on, it was reported that the barricades had been abandoned, that there was no resistance, as a result of which the units did not proceed any further. There was no reason for their further engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you have inherent authority as a represent of the minister - which is how you describe yourself - to stop or pause the operation?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't either stop or pause the operation. Measures were undertaken to remove from the barricades members of the terrorist organisation, following which there were no further reasons to proceed with the operation because there was no resistance --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and the entire police action was aimed against terrorists, not against anybody else. So it's not as though I was authorised to stop the operation. The operation's raison d'etre did not exist any longer. There was no reason to proceed with it, and this is how it ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not sure you understood the question I asked you. Did you recall the question I asked you?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you have inherent authority as the representative of the minister to stop or pause the operation? Either you did or you did not.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have such authority nor did I use such an authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in respect to the same operation, I think you were shown a document, D429.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at it, please. And before it comes up, could the document pages 41 and 42 of the document with 65 ter number 00948, could those be marked for identity?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You recall that document?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, please stop. Please stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, we're moving on from the document that's on the screen, is that intended?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I went a little bit too fast, but I was asking that the previous document that was on the screen be marked for identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. You mean there the record of the interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I don't propose to ask that the entire thing, just those two pages that you were shown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- pages 41 and 42.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Pages 41 and 42 of the interview given in 2002, yes, they will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, as Exhibit P1507, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the document on the screen at the moment, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand what is it that we marked for identification. Haven't we said that those interviews cannot be admitted into evidence? They cannot even be marked for identification. The accused can be asked about circumstances surrounding it, but I don't understand what is it that we have just marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What we have marked for identification was those passages which the accused was asked to read in the course of his evidence, so that when it comes to re-examination; when it comes to final addresses; and if it should arise, when it comes to appeal, there will be a record of precisely what it was the witness was commenting on, if that should become an issue. You will recall, Mr. Djurdjic, that a document marked for identification is not in evidence, it is not part of the evidence, it is merely a record of something that was used in the hearing. If it is admitted into evidence, it becomes then an exhibit and it is part of the case relevant to your client's guilt or innocence; but marked for identification is not. Okay? Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before you, Mr. Djordjevic, is D429. That is a document dated the 14th of September, 1998, sent by Mr. Lukic. And he complains that one Anne Delforge, a representative of the international Red Cross from the Belgrade mission, was present and she warned the refugees on several occasions and asked the people present not to return to their homes because it was not safe, thus causing panic insecurity and uncertainty among the residents on whether or not to return. And your comment about this was that certain organisations, having their own agendas, wanted to prevent the civilians to accept the offer of the police to return. That was your evidence. Did you meet this lady and find out what her complaints were?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received -- or, rather, I became familiar with this dispatch for the first time here. It deals with mid-September --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- before this operation --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand that you have a lot that you want to explain, but, for the time being, just focus on my question. Either you met the lady and discussed the complaints that she might have had or you did not meet her.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On what basis did you conclude that certain organisations like the ICRC had an agenda to prevent civilians accepting the offer of the police to return?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I spent several months down there and I was present in many instances involving other organisations, say the Association of Physicians, in whose vehicles we found weapons that they were distributing to terrorists. This is what I had in mind when I said that certain humanitarian international organisations abused their position and in some way assisted terrorists or in some other way acted inappropriately. And it is in that sense that Sreten Lukic wrote this to the minister, describing the conduct of a representative of the Red Cross. All of us there were familiar, all of us in RJB and RDB were familiar with their conduct in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So when you made the comment about having their agendas to prevent the return of the people, you were referring and you asked about this document. I take it that you had no information from Ms. Delforge about what or the reasons she may have had to do what she did? You don't have any basis to say that, what you just said, about the ICRC representative?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave a comment on this note and the information that was available to the department about her conduct at that particular point in time. I personally never met this lady. I said that I was familiar with activities of other international organisations that looked benevolently upon the activities of the terrorist organisations down there in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Shaun Byrnes gave evidence and some of his evidence, if I might give the reference, is contained in P1214 at pages 26 to 28. And he referred to the same operation -- or at least an operation in September in the same area. And he said: "The Serbian police force launched an operation against a number of villages to the south-east of Pec. They drove the residents out of the village. The international press focused particularly on the large number of displaced Albanians. In response, the MUP sent forces to the area where these people were gathered and effectively herded them home. We complained to General Lukic about the way it was done. Many of these people were terrified and had no idea what was going to happen to them, particularly if they were being herded onto MUP buses?" In September of 1998 during these operations, were you not aware of these complaints by the international organisations and the international press about the Serb MUP forces forcefully herding civilians home?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In your question, you put to me a large piece of information which is not true from the first word. Shaun Byrnes claims that Serbian security forces started an operation against some villages. That's not true. It was never done. It is true that there were many civilians in the village of Istinic, and both the MUP and the army forces had the duty when coming upon a large number of civilians to return those civilians to their homes. And it was done not once but on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, again you don't seem to understand the question. I was not asking whether or not you agree with the truth or otherwise of what Mr. Byrnes said. I was just reminding you of what he said and asking you, having regard to that and this document you see in front of you about what the ICRC representative was saying, do you recall that in September of 1998 there were complaints made in the international press and by international organisations about your MUP forces herding terrified civilians back to their home? And this was done in response to the publicity surrounding the displaced persons. Were you aware of these complaints then?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no specific concrete complaints. I was aware that due to anti-terrorist activities and combat against -- combat against the terrorist forces, that, as a result of that, civilians were leaving their homes and going to areas that they believed were safer or simply following the orders coming from terrorist organisations. I also am familiar that the international press and some representatives were concerned about the civilians who were in some areas where they believed they would be safer. However, following activities aimed against terrorists and following neutralisation of terrorists, we wanted these civilians to go back to their homes; and to that end we assisted them in returning to their homes and going back to their normal lives as much as possible. There was no mistreatment of civilians in this process. What was important for us just, just as it was in Istinic, was that these people could not remain in that other village. They needed to go back to their homes. So I don't see what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, weren't MUP forces under your command involved in forcing civilians home after this -- after their -- sorry, in forcing refugees home after the international press began to publish stories about the large number of refugees? Since I made a mistake, I'll just rephrase the question and just put it this way: Weren't MUP forces involved in forcing civilians home?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really can't understand what you're saying, to force civilians to go home. The civilians wanted to go home. The police forces and the army forces that encountered them in some rugged terrain would talk to them, try to persuade them to go back to their homes because it was safe --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that they should really lead a normal life. There was no force involved. Nobody was forced to go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But this is pretty much, Mr. Djordjevic, what Mr. Byrnes and the ICRC representative was saying. Shall we, therefore, move on then to P886. Could we look at that document quickly.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just say, this document that refers to this lady, whatever her name is, and what Mr. Byrnes was talking about, we're talking about two different events. One was in mid-September and what Mr. Byrnes is speaking about is what happened in late September, at the end of September. So these are two unrelated events. But they refer to more or less the same area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we go to page 73 in English, page 75 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These are the meeting notes of the Joint Command. You were shown these before. If you look at the note for the 4th of September, you will see that you said: "Return all the inhabitants to the village by force tomorrow ..." Are you telling us now you don't know about returning them by force? But isn't that what you ordered as a member of the Joint Command because of international press, and isn't that what these international organisations were complaining about?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now you ask me ten questions all wrapped up in one. First of all, what it says here "return all inhabitants to the village by force tomorrow," I think that Djakovic who kept the minutes here explained what he really meant. This is just his vision of things -- well, the question is: What is it that I actually said at the time? But our demands, our opinions, and our position regarding the civilians was that they should go back to their villages as soon as possible, they were not to remain in the woods. And whenever civilians were encountered - and I often was in this situation - we -- the civilians were talked to. And after they were talked to, they would go back to their homes and they were quite pleased about it. In some cases, they -- the KLA exerted control over them and would not let them go back --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, please focus on my question. Okay. You are saying that that is not what you meant. That's the answer. That's the answer you want to give.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not what I said. That -- or, rather, I didn't say that I didn't mean it. First of all, Djakovic noted down what he thought he had heard. He gave us his -- it was his spin on the words. And he spoke about that. My interest and the interest of all the people who were there was for all the villagers that had left their villages to go back and to lead normal lives. We didn't want them to be under the influence of the terrorists. So this was the gist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't issue any orders -- well, I don't know what to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, could we look at another passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's go to page 79 in English, which is page 82 in B/C/S, another Joint Command meeting in that time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djakovic recorded you as saying that a company should go to Sedlare sector and force the people to return to their villages another time, another day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, we are looking for the meeting, please, of the 6th of September, and I think it's page 79 in the B/C/S -- sorry, page 79 in the English, page 82 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, your statement that this was the Joint Command and that some things were being done there --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- well, it was not the Joint Command --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These are Mr. Djakovic's notes of what he called Joint Command meetings, and he records you to have said one company is to go to Sedlare sector and force the people to return to their villages. Now, Mr. Djordjevic, you told us that you didn't know about forcing people to return, but isn't this what the International Commission of the Red Cross and the KVM were complaining about, your orders to force the people to return in response to the international publicity?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have told you that I have some general knowledge of the opinion that prevailed among the representatives of the international community and the concern of the international community for the refugees and displaced persons in light of the terrorist actions in Kosovo. We shared their concern for the civilians who had left their homes, and we took measures to make sure that these people would go back to their homes. And we also had in mind the position of the international community vis-à-vis this problem. When I was in the field, I merely launched an initiative. The gist was that whenever we encountered civilians in the woods, they should be told to go back. So this was an initiative on my part on one of the occasions when the information was exchanged. I thought that this was a good way for the inhabitants of that one village to go back to their homes. The next day there was another briefing where it was said that the police that had gone to the village -- to that area to bring the villagers back, the villagers told them that the KLA did not allow them to go back to their homes. So this was the whole event --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the two sides of the same story.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But what Mr. Djakovic records here, you recall that you said that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember that when I look at it. Not that I actually remember it now. I remember the places where I myself was and what I did --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but these forces, the police and the army, did not force the villagers to flee their homes; --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: –- rather, they wanted to have them return to their homes from where they had fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- please just focus on my questions for the present. And you will recall, Mr. Djordjevic - and this is how it appears to me - that you were issuing an order, a directive, as to what should be done?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What directive?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you said what General Djakovic recorded you as having said, that one company is to go to the Sedlare sector and force the people to return to their villages, you were, in fact, Mr. Djordjevic, issuing an order?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. In light of what I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I proposed that the issue be dealt with in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directive, pish-pash.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 20 minutes past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When did Mr. Stevanovic cease to command the PJPs?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minute he was appointed assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry. Could we have a look at P263, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While it's coming up, did you have any special responsibilities in respect to the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The special unit in 1981 when I was chief of a section within the police administration was directly linked to my section. So from this time we have had this special relationship, if I may say so, because it was a unit within my administration, both within the police section and within the police administration. Later on, it became an independent unit, and its use and all other matters came directly under the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the minister of interior -- did he not at any time assign you responsibility for the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in what sense you mean. This unit was essentially part of public security department. So just like in relation to all other organisational units within my department, I was responsible in relation to that unit as well. But as for having any special responsibilities vis-à-vis that unit, no. Whenever there was a need in terms of commanding that unit, they would approach me as chief of the department, and then I, in turn, would approach the minister whenever there was a need to ensure equipment, materiel, weaponry, and so on. So they would come to me in those cases and if they had any other needs. And then I, in turn, would go to the minister with a specific request for the needs of that unit or the needs of any other organisational unit within my department to ensure that that unit was ready to act as needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. That was a rather long answer which went beyond the question I asked, but you said something interesting. That: "Just like in relation to all other organisational units within my department, I was responsible for that unit as well." You agree with me that you were responsible for all other units within the department, apart from the SAJ, in 1999? And I'm just quoting what you just said.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see what's contentious there --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You just said --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I was chief of the department of public security. And pursuant to the enactment on organisation of that department, all organisational units within that department came under me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Right. And the words you used was "I was responsible for them." You agree with that? You don't take that back? You were responsible for them as the head of the unit, as the head of the section?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to regular duties based on the law, I was the head of that department. And when it comes to regular duties and tasks, pursuant to that enactment I was their superior. Later on, there were certain specific additional circumstances relative to the dispatch I have here in front of me. But, fine, it’s a separate issue. What I’m saying now pertains to the enactment on organisation and staffing table.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. First question I asked you on resumption was - I'm sorry - what General Stevanovic was in charge -- whether he was in charge of the PJPs and up until when. And you said up until he became an assistant minister. This document of the 4th of June is by the minister himself. And you see in the second paragraph it says: "Major-General Zekovic and Major-General Stevanovic were appointed assistant ministers of the interior at a session of the Republic of Serbia government held on the 4th of June." So that is when he ceased to be in charge of the PJP; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were appointed at the session of the government, on the 4th of June; they were appointed assistant ministers --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, I'm just trying to save time. I -- not that what you're saying is wrong -- I'm -- I just wanted to know of the time. And these were the assignments that the minister made to the assistant ministers. Who was assigned to traffic, do you know? because I don't see it here. And I know that the traffic administration is one of the organisational units at the seat of the headquarters, but who was assigned to be in charge of traffic? Did it come under any of these portfolios?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister wrote this and sent it to everybody on the ground. At that same time, he appointed me acting chief of the department, which was the first and last time that this happened within the police --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- he also ordered me verbally that I would be responsible for the traffic police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is your answer. And that's all he assigned you to?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a complete answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that all he assigned you to?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion, he also ordered me, he also assigned me to co-ordinate the work of all secretariats in the territory of the Republic of Serbia. These other assistants mentioned here were also tasked by him for some additional matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Didn't he task you orally or otherwise with special responsibility for the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't assign any responsibility to me vis-à-vis the SAJ. It was an independent unit. But its functioning was linked to me in the sense everything that related to their functioning before they were ordered to be engaged somewhere. So in that sense, I was also responsible for the special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, where were you living in 2004?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in Budva, in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall that in 2004 or thereabouts you sent off a letter to the publisher or the editor of a newspaper in Serbia - and I might get the pronunciation wrong, but I will try nonetheless - the "Nedeljni Telegraf"?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It was -- where did you send that letter from? Where was it posted from?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave it to a friend, who took it to Moscow and then mailed it from Moscow to the editor of the "Telegraf."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you have any issues with telling us the name of that friend? If you don't want to, just say so.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's unimportant. I can give you the name, but it's not important.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember the date you wrote it or the approximate date you wrote the letter?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The month?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Right now I can't remember. If you look at the date when it was published, then it was perhaps some ten days prior to it that it had reached the editor's office and then it was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in that letter you sought to clarify your position in respect to rumours that were circulating about you in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at 65 ter 06 -- this is another one that was admitted pursuant to the recent order. It's P1474.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's the letter? That's the front page, first page, of the letter?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you signed it?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we go back to the first page of it. Towards the bottom in English and also in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said -- you were referring to the appointments that the minister made, and you referred to the administration and portfolios that the other assistant ministers had been assigned to. And in the last bullet point you said: "The minister placed me in charge of the traffic police administration and the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit." Is what you said in this letter true?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that he tasked me orally for the traffic police administration, and he also tasked me to take care of the anti-terrorist unit so that it would be properly equipped and ready to carry out assignments. As I have said to you, for a number of years prior to that, that Special Anti-Terrorist Unit was a smaller organisational unit of a larger one, headed by me. So prior to that, for some ten years, that unit was under my direct leadership, unless I'm mistaken. The oral task that I received in relation to the special unit was simply to ensure all the necessary conditions for that unit to work efficiently. That meant that if they had any requirements for any needs, they would come to me, and I, in turn, would go to the minister. As for the use of that unit, it is a separate issue, specially regulated by law. The minister in addition to that asked me --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to –- maintain contact with all the chiefs of secretariats. I was not happy with that, but what can you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- I'm sorry to interrupt you, I really am, and what you're saying is quite interesting. But please focus on my question. I am referring you to what you wrote in your letter. What you wrote is that the minister placed me in charge --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have any objections, but listening to the interpretation that I'm receiving and looking at the transcript, I would like to ask the accused to speak slower so that the interpreters can keep up and interpret everything that he's saying so that it can be recorded. That's all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It says here: "The minister placed me in charge of the ... Special Anti-Terrorist Unit." Now, you have already agreed with me that you wrote that. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's true. I did write that, and I explained in some detail how and what obligations I was charged with by him. So those were tasks relate to the overall readiness of the unit for any future tasks.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Sometimes the answers of the witness are not recorded fully because the Prosecution interrupts the answer -- the interpretation of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I do apologise. I'll try to do that only when absolutely necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, when did you -- withdrawn. I'll ask the question this way: Did you cease to be in charge of the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit during your tenure in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the moment when I was appointed the chief of the public security department -- or, rather, the acting chief up until the end of my tenure there, I was responsible for the special unit and for all the other organisational units within the RJB in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I just read this answer and tell me if it's recorded correctly. I'm asking you about the -- well, let me just read the answer first. "From the moment when I was appointed chief of the public security department -- or, rather, the acting chief up until the end of my tenure there, I was responsible for the anti-terrorist unit and for all the other organisational units within the RJB in the ministry." Is that what you just said?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not what I said. That was the interpretation. I didn't say until the end of my career. I said for as long as I was the chief of the public security department, and that's until sometime in January 2001, that was the period in which this unit was responsible to me. It was connected to me. I was responsible for that unit and for all the other units that were part of the public security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. During 1998 and 1999, did you keep a work notebook or a diary?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you told us what your radio call-sign was in Belgrade. Can you just spell it for us, please.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Morava, M-o-r-a-v-a, 2 or maybe 3; I don't recall what number it was. Morava 2 or Morava 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like to go quickly into another matter which I need some clarification -- well, which I think you could clarify. You told us yesterday at page 9721 that when Mr. Golubovic, the SUP chief from Bor, called you and told you that there were bodies or corpses there, you informed the minister of everything that the chief of secretariat told you. You said, and I will quote: "So immediately upon learning it, I informed the minister about it." Is that true, that when Mr. Golubovic told you about these bodies you informed the minister immediately; or did you give Mr. Golubovic instructions before -- let's -- let me break it down. These are two questions. Let me ask you: Is what I quoted to you, your evidence, is it true?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I didn't issue any orders until the minister was informed; and, later on, I relayed the minister's orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the 21st of January this year you made a statement to this Court that -- and I'll read it: "I first learned of the truck with the bodies from the chief of the SUP in Bor, not knowing how the truck got to be in the Danube, where it had come from, or who had organised the transport. After receiving this information, I thought that the regular police crime investigation had to be carried out in accordance with the law, and this is what I insisted upon in my conversation with the chief of the SUP in Bor." What you told us in -- on the 21st and 22nd of January is not entirely true, is it?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After receiving this information, the initial information, what I received from Caslav, it was an event of such magnitude that I couldn't make any decisions. I may have said that the crime police should look into what was going on in the field, but I said that he should wait until he hears from me and until I relay to him any order. So it's possible that at that time a remark was made that the situation should be kept under control and that the crime police should be involved and that detailed instructions would be relayed to him after I get the orders. Because the incident was of such magnitude that I myself could not make any decisions as to what should be done in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You know, I asked you two times whether or not you made any suggestions or statements or orders to Mr. Golubovic before you spoke to the minister and two times you told me no. You now say that you might have done that. And is that evidence now true, that you might have said something or given him some suggestion before you spoke to the minister?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No orders, no orders in the sense of what should be done before I consulted the minister were not issued to him by me. So I informed the minister about the incident or the event, and then I relayed his orders, and I acted in accordance with the orders that I received from the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You also said yesterday that you did not know how the people -- how and where these corpses were dug up. Who told you or how did you become aware that some of these corpses had been disinterred or dug up?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I said that I didn't know where those people had been killed or whether they had been buried or whether they had been exhumed. I knew nothing about that at all. I learned about the bodies the moment when the SUP chiefs informed me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. It might well be a problem with the translation. I'll read your testimony at 92 -- sorry, 9725 from lines 23 -- from line 23 and the following lines. "I had nothing to do with this business, neither did I know how these people died nor where they were buried, where and how they were dug up, and how they were transported." In other words, you were not saying, according to this, that you did not know whether they had been buried and whether they had been dug up; you're saying you did not know where they had been buried and where and how they had been dug up. Were you told that they had been buried, and were you told that they had been disinterred?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I did not have any information whatsoever as to how they were killed or whether they were buried or exhumed -- I didn't know anything about that until those bodies showed up and when I received information from the SUP chiefs. I never received any information to that effect. Had I been aware of it, had anyone reported to me about that, you would have heard about it here, it would already be here at the Tribunal. So I didn't have any information as to what was going on in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was just quoting the record of what I thought you said and asking about it. You also said in respect to that matter that the minister told you upon your inquiry that there were events in Kosovo - I'd like to find the correct quote -- I'm sorry, please hold on. Yes. Upon your inquiry and your pressing the issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Page and line?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you, Your Honours. This is page 9723 from about line -- from about line 24 onto the next page. Very well. Time is going.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that: "The minister made it known to me that he was fully behind it that certain incidents had happened down there," and that's in Kosovo, "and that something should be done in order to prevent the revelation of the finding of these bodies because of the NATO campaign and the bombing." Did he not tell you what the incidents were?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't mention anything specific. He just said that those were isolated incidents down there and that in light of what had happened and in light of the fact that the air-strikes were in progress, that he stood behind this whole activity regarding the emergence of those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What does that mean that "he stood behind this whole activity regarding the emergence of these bodies"?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to clear this up, to get to the bottom of it, and I insisted on that. And I proposed that a group be set up to determine what had really happened so that we would be fully aware of what was going on, what had happened. And when he saw my determination, he simply cut the story short by saying that he stood behind it and I should not be concerned with it anymore, but that I should just comply with his orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn then until tomorrow afternoon at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 9th day of December, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.03 p.m.,
